interviewcake_second-largest-item-in-bst.walkthrough: In the tree [12,5,20,2,9,17,25], the rightward search visits 12, 20 and 25. Node 25 has no left subtree, so its parent, 20, is the second-largest key. The tree remains unchanged.

interviewcake_stock-price.walkthrough: For prices [11,7,13,4,10], the first feasible profit is 7-11=-4. Price 7 becomes the cheapest earlier purchase; selling at 13 improves the profit to 6. The later low price 4 followed by 10 also gives 6. Updating the minimum only after considering a sale prevents buying and selling at the same position.

interviewcake_balanced-binary-tree.walkthrough: For [4,2,7,1,3,null,9], the leaves are 1, 3 and 9. Each is two edges below the root, so the shallowest and deepest depths are both 2 and their difference is 0. Return true. A long chain would also return true because it has only one leaf.

interviewcake_bst-checker.walkthrough: For [10,4,16,1,7,12,19], node 4 inherits an upper bound of 10; its right child 7 must lie strictly between 4 and 10. Node 16 inherits a lower bound of 10, and its left child 12 must lie between 10 and 16. Every inherited interval is respected, so the answer is true.

interviewcake_bracket-validator.walkthrough: Scanning a{b[c](d)}, ignore letters and push {, then [. The ] removes [, the ( is pushed and removed by ), and the final } removes {. No closer crosses another pair and the stack finishes empty, so return true.

interviewcake_cafe-order-checker.walkthrough: For takeOut=[8,3], dineIn=[5,9], served=[5,8,3,9], consume 5 from the dine-in head, then 8 and 3 from takeout, then 9 from dine-in. Both source positions reach their ends exactly, so return true.

interviewcake_nth-fibonacci.walkthrough: For n=6, start with F(0)=0 and F(1)=1. Advancing the two running values produces 1, 2, 3, 5 and 8 for indices 2 through 6. The required result is 8; there is no recursive tree of repeated work.

interviewcake_delete-node.walkthrough: The list is 9 -> 4 -> 7 -> 2 and the supplied target is the node currently holding 4. Copy 7 into that same target object and point it to the node holding 2. The head-to-tail values become [9,7,2]. An alias to the target now observes 7, while an alias to the bypassed successor still refers to its separate, unchanged object.

interviewcake_linked-list-cycles.walkthrough: For values [2,2,9] with tail link -1, the last node points to null. The repeated payload 2 does not imply a cycle: the two nodes are different objects. The fast pointer reaches the end, so return false.

interviewcake_find-duplicate-files.walkthrough: The controlled directory contains a.txt and nested/b.txt, both with the bytes "same bytes". Their sizes and all three bounded samples match. Their modification times are 1000 and 2000, so report their full paths with a.txt first as the earlier-time candidate. This orientation is a heuristic, and equal fingerprints can still be false positives; neither file is changed.

interviewcake_find-duplicate-optimize-fo.walkthrough: For [1,3,4,2,3], candidate values are 1..4. The lower half 1..2 contains two entries, fitting its two slots, so continue in 3..4. Value 3 alone appears twice but has only one available slot; narrowing finishes at 3. Every pass reads the same unchanged input.

Treat index i as pointing to numbers[i]. In [4,1,3,4,2], the path from index 0 is 0 -> 4 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4, with cycle entry 4. Slow and fast pointers meet in that cycle; moving one pointer back to 0 and advancing both identifies entry 4, a repeated array value.

interviewcake_find-rotation-point.walkthrough: For [mint,oak,ant,birch,cedar], compare the middle word ant with the upper-end word cedar. The minimum is in the left portion including ant. The next comparison places mint before the wrap and moves the lower bound to index 2. Both bounds then identify ant, so return 2.

interviewcake_graph-coloring.walkthrough: For the triangle with adjacency [[1,2],[0,2],[0,1]] and palette [red,blue,green], assign red to v0, blue to v1 because v0 is red, and green to v2 because its neighbors use both red and blue. Every edge has different endpoint colors. Any other valid assignment also passes; the displayed true reports successful properties.

interviewcake_highest-product-of-3.walkthrough: For [-8,-5,2,4], the first two negatives have product 40. Combining that pair with 2 gives 80, and later with 4 gives 160. Selecting the three numerically largest values would miss this result; tracking both low and high pair products preserves the winning candidate.

interviewcake_queue-two-stacks.walkthrough: Enqueue 4 and 9 into the incoming stack. The first Dequeue moves them to the outgoing stack and removes 4. Enqueue 2 without moving the still-pending 9. The next Dequeue removes 9; only then does transferring the incoming stack expose 2. The returned values are 4, 9 and 2 in FIFO order.

interviewcake_shuffle.walkthrough: Starting with [4,8,1], position 0 chooses uniformly among all three occurrences. If it selects index 2, the array becomes [1,8,4]. Position 1 then chooses index 1 or 2 equally, producing [1,8,4] or [1,4,8]. Each full three-element permutation has probability 1/(3*2)=1/6. The judge returns true when these distribution and in-place properties hold.

interviewcake_inflight-entertainment.walkthrough: For movieLengths=[35,60,45,20] and flightLength=80, remember 35, then 60. At duration 45, the needed complement is 35, which is already from a different position, so return true. A single duration 40 would not be enough by itself.

interviewcake_kth-to-last-node-in-singly.walkthrough: For k=2 and list 5 -> 8 -> 1 -> 6, advance the leading pointer two nodes to 1. Move both pointers together until the leading pointer passes the tail; the following pointer then refers to the original node holding 1. Its zero-based identity index is 2, which is the adapter output; the method returns that node object.

interviewcake_largest-stack.walkthrough: Push 5, then 9. The auxiliary maximum stack records both increases, so GetMax returns 9. Pop removes 9 from both stacks. The remaining maximum is 5, and the next GetMax reads it without removing it. Equal maxima would each need a retained occurrence as well.

interviewcake_coin.walkthrough: For amount 8 and denominations [2,3,5], the three unordered combinations are 2+2+2+2, 2+3+3, and 3+5. Processing each denomination in the outer loop adds each combination once; 5+3 is the same combination as 3+5, not a fourth answer.

interviewcake_merge-sorted-arrays.walkthrough: Merge [1,4,4] and [2,4,9] by repeatedly taking the smaller head: 1, then 2, then the three occurrences of 4, then 9. The new output is [1,2,4,4,4,9]; neither input is sorted again or modified.

interviewcake_merging-ranges.walkthrough: Sort [[9,12],[1,4],[4,7],[10,14]] by start to obtain [1,4], [4,7], [9,12], [10,14]. The first two touch and become [1,7]. The last two overlap and become [9,14]. The gap from 7 to 9 remains, giving [[1,7],[9,14]] in newly allocated meeting objects.

interviewcake_mesh-message.walkthrough: In the network a:{b,c}, b:{a,d}, c:{a,d}, d:{b,c}, breadth-first search visits b and c at distance 1 and discovers d at distance 2. Reconstructing via b gives [a,b,d]. The equally short route [a,c,d] is also valid; both contain two edges.

interviewcake_compress-url-list.walkthrough: Insert https://a/b: create missing character links and mark its final node, returning true. Insert https://a next: its character path exists, but its final node was not a complete key, so return true. Repeating https://a/b returns false. Extending it to https://a/b/c marks a different complete key and returns true.

interviewcake_matching-parens.walkthrough: In x(ab(cd)e)y, the opener at index 1 starts depth 1. The opener at index 4 increases depth to 2, its closer at index 7 reduces it to 1, and the closer at index 9 reduces it to 0. Return index 9 rather than the first closing parenthesis.

interviewcake_permutation-palindrome.walkthrough: For aabbc, toggling odd-frequency membership removes a after its second occurrence and removes b after its second. Only c remains odd. It can occupy the middle of a palindrome such as abcba, so return true without enumerating reorderings.

interviewcake_product-of-other-numbers.walkthrough: For [2,0,-3,4], the left-product pass writes [1,2,0,0]. Multiplying right products into those entries gives [0,-24,0,0]. At the zero position, the other values multiply to 2*(-3)*4=-24; every other position includes the zero. Division is unnecessary.

interviewcake_rectangular-love.walkthrough: Rectangle [1,2,6,4] spans x=1..7 and y=2..6; [4,0,5,4] spans x=4..9 and y=0..4. The common x interval is 4..7 and the common y interval is 2..4, so return a new rectangle [4,2,3,2]. Both dimensions are positive.

interviewcake_recursive-string-permutati.walkthrough: For ab, recurse on b to obtain the set {b}. Insert a before b and after b, yielding {ab,ba}. The base case for an empty suffix is the singleton set containing the empty string, which makes the first insertion possible.

interviewcake_reverse-linked-list.walkthrough: For nodes 3 -> 8 -> 1, first set node 3.Next to null. Next point the original node 8 to node 3, then point the original node 1 to node 8. Return the original node holding 1. The resulting values are [1,8,3], with every payload still attached to its original object.

interviewcake_reverse-string-in-place.walkthrough: For the mutable characters of cloud, exchange c with d, then l with u; the middle o stays in place. The same array now contains duolc. No replacement array is returned.

interviewcake_reverse-words.walkthrough: For foxes run fast, reversing all characters gives tsaf nur sexof. Reverse each space-delimited segment in that same array to restore the internal spelling, producing fast run foxes. Spaces remain separators and the array length is unchanged.

interviewcake_simulate-5-sided-die.walkthrough: With injected draws 6, 7, 3, reject 6 and 7 and return 3. In general each accepted source value 1..5 has the same source probability, so conditioning on acceptance gives probability 1/5. The judge output true denotes passed range, source-use and probability properties, not a fixed rolled value.

interviewcake_simulate-7-sided-die.walkthrough: For injected draws 5,5,1,1, the first pair creates state (5-1)*5+(5-1)=24, which is rejected. The next pair creates state 0 and returns 1. Among accepted states 0..20, each remainder modulo seven occurs three times, giving probability 1/7 for each output. The displayed true reports the judge properties.

interviewcake_temperature-tracker.walkthrough: Insert 4, 10 and 4. The minimum is 4, maximum 10, sum 18 and count 3, so the mean is 6. Frequency 4 is 2 while frequency 10 is 1, so GetMode returns 4. Repeating getters does not consume any reading.

interviewcake_cake-thief.walkthrough: For types [weight=3,value=7] and [weight=5,value=13] with capacity 11, choose one weight-5 item and two weight-3 items. Total weight is 11 and value is 13+7+7=27. Two weight-5 items yield only 26; three weight-3 items yield 21. The unbounded dynamic program reuses earlier capacity optima to find 27.

interviewcake_find-unique-int-among-dupl.walkthrough: For [14,3,14,8,3], XOR combines equal pairs to zero: 14^14=0 and 3^3=0. Since XOR is associative and commutative, the final accumulator equals 8, the only identifier without a cancelling partner.

interviewcake_top-scores.walkthrough: For scores [3,8,3,0,5] and K=8, the count table records one 8, one 5, two 3s and one 0. Reading counts from score 8 down to 0 emits [8,5,3,3,0] in a new array. Both occurrences of 3 are retained.

interviewcake_which-appears-twice.walkthrough: For [3,1,4,2,3], n is length-1=4. The expected sum 1+2+3+4 is 10, while the actual sum is 13. Their difference is 3, the duplicated value. Use widened arithmetic for the sum and formula before subtracting.

interviewcake_word-cloud.walkthrough: For "Owls fly; OWLS don't crawl. Fly-by owls!", punctuation ends tokens but internal apostrophes and letter-surrounded hyphens remain. Lowercasing combines Owls, OWLS and owls into count 3. The other keys are fly, don't, crawl and fly-by, each counted once under the disclosed bank policy.

arguments: Owls fly; OWLS don't crawl. Fly-by owls!
